problem: Vision-based navigation policies (online or offline RL) rely on hand-engineered rewards that need domain expertise, heavy tuning and LiDAR/depth for obstacle distance. Pairwise Bradley-Terry preference learning gives noisy, coarse signals.
motivation: Human intuition about navigability and social compliance is hard to formalize as a reward, yet it could let cheap RGB-only robots navigate safely. Large real-world datasets (SCAND) contain expert behavior that can be turned into a preference-aligned reward without online interaction.
key_idea: Learn an action-conditioned, goal-independent visual reward from RGB by ranking a local grid of candidate (v, ω) actions with Boltzmann preference scores derived from binary human feasibility answers, and training with the Plackett-Luce loss.
insight: The reward model is a general component: plugged into offline IQL or as a DWA/MPC cost term it gives large gains over hand-engineered LiDAR-based rewards (e.g. Scenario 3 IQL: HER 0% vs HALO 80% SR). The learned reward transfers to unseen scenes and hardware, and the same reward works better with IQL than with TD3-BC, showing that the policy learner still matters (HALO+TD3-BC only 10% in scenarios 1 and 3). No ablations of the reward model components are reported.
method: Preference data: 5 binary queries per frame (turn left/right, decelerate, accelerate, danger/suboptimal), annotated on 25 SCAND scenes (~107k frames) plus 116 self-collected legged-robot scenes (~33k frames, ~100 truncated unsafe negatives); a danger flag replaces the reference action with a corrective one.

Boltzmann preference scoring: 5x5 grid of (v, ω) around the reference action, separable Boltzmann distributions with adaptive temperatures (preferred direction gets ≥95% of the mass), scaled by λ (positive 1+ΣU, or negative -1/(1+ΣU) when danger) and ranked, with the reference on top.

Plackett-Luce loss: negative log-likelihood of the ranking over all 25 candidate actions, avoiding pairwise comparisons; auxiliary reward-diversity hinge, focal regression and L2 regularizers (λ=2.0, 0.05, 0.01 respectively).

Reward architecture: frozen DINOv2 (ViT-S, 256 patches × 384) followed by transformer self-attention layers; the action is projected via homography to a 32×32 binary path mask, a small CNN turns it into a sigmoid spatial weight map that multiplies the patch embeddings, and an MLP outputs the scalar reward.
Offline policy: goal-conditioned IQL and TD3-BC (CORL implementation) with a DINOv2 encoder and mean-pooled patches, using the HALO reward with goal distance/heading terms (λ_halo=1/5).
MPC/DWA integration: adds -λ_halo·R_HALO to a DWA cost (goal, heading, smoothness; no obstacle term), 1 s horizon, 5 Hz, 25 sampled velocities.

numbers_note: Metric key NTL = normalized trajectory length, Frechet = Fréchet distance (m) to the human teleop trajectory. Only real-world Husky results on 3 scenarios with 10 trials each; no standard benchmark; no ablations of reward components. HALO + TD3-BC rows (SR 10/70/10) omitted.
results: HALO + IQL reaches 80/90/80% success across the three real-world scenarios, versus HER + IQL 50/10/0% and DWA (LiDAR) 80/100/0%, and VANP 60/60% in the two scenarios it was run. HALO + DWA gives the lowest Fréchet distance in Scenario 1 (0.892). The abstract claims ≥33.3% higher SR, 12.9% lower normalized length and 26.6% lower Fréchet distance versus SOTA vision baselines.
limitations: Small real-world evaluation (10 trials per scenario, 3 scenarios) with no reward-model ablations; results depend strongly on the policy learner (TD3-BC is poor).
Inconsistent across checkpoints and sensitive to lighting; not explainable.
Limited field of view causes object impermanence and lack of awareness of robot width, so it fails in tight clearances.
